consensus_summary: All four blind responses converge on the same core: the 'new name' symbolizes a new, God-given identity, character, and status conferred on the redeemed person or people — transformation, covenant belonging, ownership by God, and eschatological vindication — grounded in the renaming pattern (Abram, Jacob, Simon), Isaiah 62/65, and Revelation 2:17 / 3:12. Debated details (secret intimacy, ownership inscription, admission/acquittal token) are treated as complementary variations on that core.
book_summary: The book identifies the new name not as a bestowed personal identity but as 'a renewed Word, covenant, and priesthood' — an objective covenantal reality that is known, received, and kept only by the one who bears the renewed Name. It explicitly flags the identity/character reading as the merely 'commonly taught' view.
consensus_core_identification: A new identity/character/status given by God to the redeemed person or people, marking transformation, belonging, and vindication.
book_core_identification: A renewed Word, covenant, and priesthood — a covenantal office/revelation held and kept privately by its bearer, rather than a transformed personal identity.
boundary_disagreement: The book applies the term to the same proof-texts (Jacob/Israel, Zion in Isaiah 62, the overcomer in Revelation 2:17) but reclassifies what the name in those texts is: not the person's renewed identity but a renewed Word/covenant/priesthood the person receives and keeps. The private-knowledge element of Rev 2:17 is retained, but its referent is shifted from personal identity to covenantal office/revelation.
material_contradiction: The consensus says the new name IS the believer's transformed identity/status; the book says it is a renewed Word, covenant, and priesthood that the bearer holds — and it explicitly sets this against the 'commonly taught' identity-and-character reading. Both cannot be the central identification of the same symbol in the same sense: an identity conferred on a person is not a covenant/priesthood entrusted to a person, and the book's framing treats the consensus view as the reading it is correcting rather than refining.
rationale: Every consensus response, and all listed alternatives (secret intimacy, divine ownership, corporate restoration, Christ's own name, literal afterlife name, admission token), stays within the category of a name-as-identity/status/belonging. None identifies the new name as a renewed Word, covenant, or priesthood. The book's explicit common-view note confirms it intends replacement of the identity reading, not elaboration of it. It preserves overlapping features (given by God, received by the overcomer, privately known per Rev 2:17, covenantal overtones per Isa 62:4-5), so extensions overlap, but the central referent is replaced — identity is exchanged for covenantal Word/priesthood. That is core-level contradiction, hence DIVERGENT rather than REFINED. It is not NOVEL in the strict sense of the verdict hierarchy because divergence (replacement of the consensus referent) takes precedence over mere absence from the alternatives list.
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED: the book keeps the broad category of 'something God bestows on the overcomer, privately known and kept' (Rev 2:17's secrecy clause and Isaiah 62's marriage/covenant imagery arguably support a covenantal reading), so the book might be seen as specifying the content of the new identity (a covenant/priesthood role) rather than replacing it. Additionally, 'covenant relationship' appears within Response A's primary meaning, giving some conceptual overlap.
